newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary wheat export prospects look gloomy - trade.
newsitem.headline: Hungary wheat export prospects look gloomy - trade.

text.p: Hungary's bumper 1997 wheat crop will leave at least 1.5 million tonnes for export but trading companies said on Thursday that so far only about one third of that amount has been contracted.
"I don't think there are export contracts for more than 500,000 tonnes," Attila Kovacs, General Manager of grains trading company Agrimpex told Reuters.
Official forecasts put this year's wheat harvest at around five million tonnes, up from last year's 3.9 million tonnes.
In 1996, Hungary had a wheat surplus of about one million tonnes, of which it exported some 250,000 tonnes.
Kovacs said that estimates of this year's wheat surplus ran from 1.5 million to 2.5 million tonnes and the government's intention to subsidise storage offered only a temporary solution.
"It could solve some immediate liquidity problems (for producers) but in the final analysis it will only put off the problem (of excess stocks)," Kovacs said.
He added that wheat export outlooks were dampened by record crop expectations in other eastern European countries.
"Romania, Yugoslavia and the Ukraine will all export wheat," Kovacs said. "These countries will turn from potential markets to competitors".

The Ukraine forecasts a winter wheat crop of 20 million tonnes, up from last year's 13.1 million tonnes, Romania expects a crop of over seven million tonnes, compared with 3.1 million tonnes in 1996, while Yugoslavia sees 2.8 million tonnes, up from a record-low of 1.5 million tonnes last year.
Robert Vajo of grains brokerage Termin said Poland, Belarus and Russia could be potential export markets for Hungary and Kovacs added that the Mediterranean region also offered some possibilities.
"North Africa has regular import needs, but Turkey and Israel are also such countries," he said.
He also said that the combined effect of expectations of a good crop and uncertain exports had already pushed wheat futures prices considerably lower.

"Near maturity wheat futures dropped to around 20,000 forints (per tonne) from about 24,000 forints two months ago," Kovacs said, adding that spot prices were around 18,000 forints but even that was high compared with European FOB prices.
"There is still tension between these prices and if international prices don't rise, then exporters will only be prepared to buy below current (Hungarian spot) prices," Kovacs said.
